subject: How to analyze data for density with Distance software

messages.author: 3e9d625f8964ade3
messages.subject: How to analyze data for density with Distance software
parts:
Hi, I'm a new user for Distance software. I still have a lack of knowledge on how to use the software and I have just started to learn it. But now it is urgent for me that I need to complete my analysis in these few days. 

I have data of trees species observed from line transect sampling from two areas of secondary forest and primary forest. I'm trying to do species density comparison between both sites. Some example of my data was shown on the table.


I have tried to run it in Distance Software, I do not really know what is the correct properties to use. Therefore, I just try all the analysis engine and got the results with a warning. So, is it the D value is reasonable to use? 

Is there any suggestion for me, how I can solve my problem? 

Thank you so much in advance!

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to analyze data for density with Distance software
parts:
Suzi

Welcome to the distance sampling list.  I can't answer all of your questions from the figures you provide.  However, I make three observations:

  • a warning message from Distance does not necessarily mean the results are incorrect; warnings are generated by the software to indicate that something seems unusual and that you should investigate more closely.  Without looking at your project, I don't know the nature of the warning, but I'll speculate about that below
  • looking at your results table, the delta-AIC scores are small for all models, meaning there is little to choose between them.  However I see that you included the negative exponential model.  It is a model without a shoulder, meaning it falls away steeply at small distances from the transect.  We usually discourage use of that model, unless the biological situation warrants.  It seems surprising to me that in sampling trees, the detection function would fall off very rapidly; but you were the data collector--you must assess whether to include the negative exponential in your model set
  • finally looking at the data table you provide, it appears that you placed only a single transect in each of your habitat type strata, for which you wish to make a comparison.  With a single transect, encounter rate variance cannot be assessed (no variability with a sample of size 1).  I suspect that may be the nature of the warning message Distance has produced.  This is a weakness of the survey design, not something that can be remedied during the analysis.  You have little standing to make inference from a single transect to the habitat you were sampling.  You will need to recognise that limitation of your work.  Perhaps I am wrong, and the image you provided is only a portion of the data you collected.
  • Given that you want to compare densities between habitats, you'll want to ask Distance to produce stratum-specific density estimates; if number of detections per habitat support it (~60), you'd want to also fit stratum-specific detection functions to ensure the stratum-specific estimates are independent.
Hopefully that is of some help.  Ask further questions if I was wrong about my guesses.

Eric Rexstad

Hi Eric, 

Thank you for your great explanations. Yeah, it's probably my lack of knowledge on distance before performing the survey design in the field where actually I have only 4 transects in total, with one in secondary forest and tree in the primary forest. I'm looking for the figs tree which was commonly found in the rich forest. During the survey, I have encounter fewer species of figs trees in the secondary forest (therefore I just did it one). While, in primary forest, I do cover different parts of the area. 
In this case, even though it might be unreasonable to do the comparison between both sites, but I would like to do just roughly density estimation of figs tree species encounter during the survey (& I have excluded the area detail, e.g size/Ha with blank during run the analysis in distance.) 

I have few more question here, I do run separately the data of secondary and primary forest in Distance, means in separate analysis of secondary and primary. I have run first the secondary and select the density which has the lowest AIC (as you have mention, the better model) and does the same with the primary forest data. 
Is it the right way to run the analysis or there is a way that runs together all data in one analysis? (Sorry for my lack of understandings on this). 

And I have a total of 60 individuals tree (50 from primary and 10 from the secondary forest). For this, I also need to fit stratum-specific detection? I do not really understand it, can you please enlighten me. Attache file is my data.

Thank you. 


 


 Suzika
Suzika Juiling

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to analyze data for density with Distance software
parts:
Suzi

Thanks for sharing your data and field experiences.

It is a bit awkward that you exerted so little effort in the secondary forest.  With only 10 detections on a single transect, there is little you can say about fig density in this habitat.  A more sound survey design would have been to allocate sampling effort into each habitat type prior to beginning to collect data, rather than choosing when to stop data collection based upon the data.

Survey design aside, one way to analysed data from two habitats is to combine them in a single Distance project, as they were part of a single study as I have done below (perpendicular distances in observation layer not shown).

I then request a stratified analysis, and density estimates for each stratum using this screen:
This will produce density estimates for each stratum using the detection function fitted with detections from each stratum.  That is a challenge here because of the small number of detections in the secondary forest stratum; but having separate detection functions makes the two density estimates independent; which they would not be if a shared detection function was fitted to the data pooled across strata.

As an aside, note your data have a strong peak at distances <1m.  There is little information about the detection function from the small number of detections > 7m.  So perhaps some truncation should be used, depleting an already small number of detections.
